about: Guidance cards: per report section, the possible causes and actions a report may show. Code shows an entry only when every clause of its `when` holds on the computed metrics; nothing else is ever shown, so every model gives the same list. A clause is [metric, op, value] with op one of < <= > >= == !=, or [metric, "status", [statuses]]. Causes are possibilities, never conclusions.

causes.text: Appliances lost contact with the Orchestrator for part of the period: a site power, ISP or management-path outage, or a reboot.
Appliances on ECOS older than 9.3.4 / 9.4.2 / 9.5.0 report no reachability samples, which reads as missing data rather than downtime.

actions.text: Open Monitoring > Availability for the appliances below target and match the down minutes with the alarm history for the same days.

causes.text: An underlay (transport) circuit was down or unstable, taking the tunnels on it down.
Tunnels stayed up but degraded (brownout): loss or latency above the overlay's SLA without a full outage.
Tunnels down for the whole period are usually unused or decommissioned paths, not outages.

actions.text: Review the tunnels listed as down all period; remove or disable the ones that are no longer meant to exist so they stop counting.
For transports below target, compare their down minutes across sites: the same circuit label failing at several sites points to the carrier.

causes.text: Paths outside the health thresholds: loss, latency or jitter on the underlying circuit, or congestion at one end.
Tunnels that carry no traffic yet lose probes are usually broken or misconfigured paths (firewall, NAT or a dead peer).

actions.text: Start with the worst paths in the table: compare pre-FEC and post-FEC loss and the transport each runs on (Monitoring > Tunnel Health).
Check the idle tunnels that lose probes in the tunnel list; fix the peer or remove the unused path.

causes.text: The circuit under these paths loses packets; FEC recovers them, so applications see little loss, but it costs extra bandwidth and fails if loss rises further.

actions.text: Check the circuits behind these paths with their carrier: the loss before FEC is the circuit's real quality.

causes.text: A change type that fails almost every time is usually a template or policy the appliance rejects, retried by the Orchestrator's automation.

actions.text: Review the failed changes in the table, newest first: a failed template or configuration push leaves the appliance different from what the Orchestrator expects.

causes.text: An alarm raised again and again on one appliance usually means a flapping link, tunnel or service rather than separate events.

actions.text: Start with the appliances at the top of the repeating-alarm table; fixing one flapping path often removes most of the alarm load.
Run `edgeconnect-mcp report store` daily so alarms older than the Orchestrator's 7 days are kept for monthly reports.

causes.text: Unreachable appliances: site power, ISP, or the management path to the Orchestrator is down.
Out-of-sync appliances have configuration that differs from what the Orchestrator expects.

actions.text: For each unreachable appliance, check whether it is planned (maintenance, decommissioned) before contacting the site.
Review out-of-sync appliances in the Orchestrator and resynchronise them after checking what differs.
Triage the critical alarms first (oldest at the top of the table), then the major ones.
Work through the major alarms grouped by appliance; one appliance with many alarms is usually one problem.

causes.text: MOS is rated unhealthy almost everywhere while loss, latency and jitter are healthy: the MOS health threshold setting is the likely cause, not the network.
Standing alarms rate every hour as unhealthy until they are cleared, even when traffic is fine.
Loss outside the threshold on some paths in the last 24 hours.

actions.text: Check the MOS thresholds in the Orchestrator's health settings (GET /health/healthThresholdConfig) against the measured MOS before treating this as an outage.
Clear or acknowledge alarms that are no longer relevant so health reflects current conditions.

causes.text: Tunnels down now: a failed transport at one end, or tunnels to appliances that are themselves unreachable.

actions.text: Start with the tunnels where one end is an unreachable appliance (the Unreachable end column): they come back with that appliance; the rest point to transport problems.
No tunnel down points at an unreachable appliance: check the transport (underlay) state at both ends.

causes.text: Links at or above the planning limit for a large share of hours: sustained demand, or a scheduled job such as backups running in business hours.

actions.text: Before ordering bandwidth, check which applications drive the busy links; QoS or rescheduling may solve it.
No link reached the planning limit: no upgrade is needed on this period's data. Recheck over a full month before deciding.
Start renewal for licences expiring within 90 days.
Look up the appliance licence expiry dates in the HPE licence portal; this report could not read them.

causes.text: Appliances without a recent backup: the scheduled backup job is off or failing for them, or they were unreachable when it ran.

actions.text: Check the scheduled backup job for appliances without a backup in 30 days.
Plan upgrades for the versions listed against advisories; read each advisory for workarounds until then.
More than one ECOS train is in use: plan to bring appliances onto one supported train.

causes.text: A zone pair dropping every flow, or a large share: an intended deny, a missing allow rule, or an interface left in the default zone.

actions.text: For each flagged pair, confirm in the Orchestrator's firewall policy that the drops are intended; add an allow rule or move the interface to the right zone if not.

causes.text: QoS drops on a link that is far from full point to a class share or shaper rate set too low, or to short bursts, rather than to too little bandwidth.

actions.text: Review the minimum bandwidth of the dropping classes in the shaper before considering an upgrade.
Most of the saving comes from two appliances: check the optimisation policy on the others (traffic may be encrypted or already compressed, or optimisation not applied).
Start with the critical alarm types at the top of the table; find their appliances in the NOC digest.
Start with the appliances rated Critical (a critical alarm raised in the window, or reachability below target), then Warning.
Work through the alarms raised in the window first, by appliance; the already-open ones were there before the incident.
Check the failed changes on the affected appliances; for a full audit trail of the window, send the audit log to a remote log receiver.
Work down the table from the highest score; unreachable appliances score highest because nothing else can be checked until they are back.
